title: New beginnings in Belgrade: What’s next for Serbia’s students - European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Serbia's student movement unseated Aleksandar Vucic after 14 years, winning 53% to SNS's 39% on record turnout, but the new government inherits captured institutions, Russia ties and an obstructive SNS. Morina urges the EU to avoid overt interference, offer reform expertise tied to Western Balkans Growth Plan funding, and expect limited change on Kosovo, Bosnia and Russia sanctions.

insights.claim: After two years of protests, Serbia's student movement won 53% of the vote against Vucic's SNS on 39% on a record turnout, ending his 14-year rule.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: A major political transition in Serbia shifts its EU and Russia alignment outlook.
insights.quote: After two years of protests, Serbia’s student movement has finally unseated Vucic, winning 53% of the vote—well ahead of his SNS party’s 39%—on a record turnout.
insights.locator: It is clear that we have lost these elections

insights.claim: The new government inherits close ties to Russia, captured media, judicial and security structures and a difficult EU relationship, while SNS remains in parliament as a likely obstructionist force.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: Reform implementation will be slow; institutional risk in Serbia stays elevated near term.

insights.claim: An SNS candidate could still win Serbia's presidential election later this year, though a democratic reset is possible if the students form a skilful governing coalition.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: Upcoming presidential vote is a key risk to the reform trajectory.

insights.claim: Europeans should resist rushing proposals onto the new Serbian government, since that would feed Vucic's claim that his defeat was due to European influence, but should insist on a transparent transfer of power.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: EU engagement will be cautious and paced.

insights.claim: The European Commission should offer expertise and financing for rule of law, anti-corruption, media ownership and electoral reform, tying Western Balkans Growth Plan funding to delivery and judging success by whether state capture is uprooted.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
entities: Growth Plan for the Western Balkans
insights.so_what: Conditional EU funds could unlock investment if Serbia delivers anti-corruption reforms.

insights.claim: A Kosovo breakthrough is unlikely because the Students' List programme pledges to 'fight to keep Kosovo as part of Serbia', though Belgrade may become less confrontational and reopen dialogue.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: Kosovo dispute will continue to constrain Serbia's EU accession.
insights.locator: Judging by the movement's statements on Kosovo

insights.claim: In Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro major changes are unlikely; with Milorad Dodik's party sweeping Republika Srpska, a more democratic Belgrade may tame its backing for Serb nationalism but not reduce the sentiment itself.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: Western Balkans regional risk remains largely unchanged despite Serbia's transition.
insights.locator: In Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro

insights.claim: The Students' List quickly reassured Moscow it would not join EU sanctions on Russia, though it is too early to tell whether this is firm policy or strategic ambiguity.
insights.speaker: Engjellushe Morina
insights.so_what: Serbia is unlikely to align with EU Russia sanctions soon, relevant for sanctions-compliance and energy exposure.
